newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rand, new finds pump up Energy Africa stock.
newsitem.headline: Rand, new finds pump up Energy Africa stock.

text.p: South African oil and gas exploration company Energy Africa Ltd is on a roll with its shares up 50 percent since its listing last March, buoyed by a weak rand, high oil prices and optimism about discoveries.
The stock hit a record high of 15.30 rand on November 6 before slipping back in a troubled overall market.
It received a further boost on Wednesday, adding 10 cents to 14.90 rand, on news of "significant" gas reserves in the Kudu-4 gas field off Namibia in which it has a 10 percent stake.

Although it will be some time before the full implications of the find are known, the field, operated by Shell Exploration and Production Namibia BV shows promise of holding more reserves than previously thought.

Analysts said the market had become attuned to the value of the former upstream arm of South African oil firm Engen Ltd since its separate listing. The group has interests in West and southern Africa.

Finance director Jim Rutland said the rising share price reflected a number of factors, notably the stock's strength as a rand hedge in an environment where the rand has this year lost 30 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar.
"The share price obviously reflects the weakening rand against the dollar...we also have one or two major discoveries, and people are getting to know us," Rutland told Reuters.
He said at current rand levels, almost 17 million rand could be added to annual turnover each time the oil price rose $1.

"Our crude oil production is now running at 10,000 barrels a day (bpd) which is more than three million barrels a year. If the oil price goes up a dollar we are better off by over $3 million," he said.

Analysts said almost all Energy Africa's operations are based outside South Africa, making it more attractive as a rand-hedge share than parent Engen, which still owns a 60.5 percent stake in its young offspring.

"All their assets other than one, the Oribi exploration block, are outside South Africa, so about 95 percent of their assets are priced in dollars. Their cash flow is also in dollars," said Themi Themistocleous, an analyst at SBC Warburg.
Oribi, in which Energy Africa has a 20 percent holding, is South Africa's first oil field. It is due to start pumping 20,000 bpd at the beginning of February.
Analysts said Energy Africa looked set for a promising future through its exploration activities in Angola, and producing operations in the North Sea and offshore Congo.
"They have secured some very exciting acreage in West Africa. The potential from that could add value to the company," Themistocleous said.

Rutland said the company had set its sights on opportunities in North Africa and was also investigating joint operations in Africa with Petronas, the Malaysian state oil and gas company which bought into parent Engen in June.
